leads.name: The Dutch Elms of Kalverbos
leads.story:
Fourteen elms stand at one corner of a park that used to be a cemetery. Kalverbos served as Delft's burial ground for 46 years before the city moved its dead to the Jaffalaan in 1874, and when the empty ground became a public park two decades later, laid out in the romantic style by garden architect Hugo Poortman, these trees were already grown. The register dates them to between 1860 and 1870, planted while this was still consecrated ground, which puts them at about 160 years old.

Four graves were left in place rather than moved, and the strangest belongs to Karl Wilhelm Naundorff, a Prussian clockmaker who spent his life insisting he was the lost Dauphin of France, Louis XVII, smuggled out of prison as a child while a substitute died in his place. Nobody believed him while he lived, and DNA testing in 2000 finally settled the argument against him, but his grave in this Dutch park still carries the fleur-de-lis of French royalty.

The elms have their own survival story. Dutch elm disease, named for the country that first identified it, swept through the Netherlands twice in the twentieth century and emptied whole streets of exactly this species. This grove made it through both waves and is now one of Delft's protected monumental groups.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1680756: Hollandse iep, fourteen trees, Hoek Kalverbos/Nieuwe Plantage, Delft, planting band 1860-1870, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, recorded as visitable and visible
leads.access: Free, in the open park of Kalverbos, at any hour
leads.transport: Delft railway station, then about a 15-minute walk
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a grove of fourteen elms, one of Delft's protected monumental groups, survivors of two waves of Dutch elm disease. They stand at one corner of Kalverbos.
leads.removed_reason: Dead or felled per the register itself: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1680756 carries status 5, Dood/geveld (checked 2026-10-10 against the Bomenstichting ArcGIS layer). Inspector remark: "In 1996/97 nog gesnoeid." Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry.

leads.name: The Ash of the Oostpoort
leads.access: Free. Public lawn beside the canal at the Oostpoort gate (plantsoen), listed visitable and visible in the register.
leads.transport: About 1 km east of Delft station, roughly 0.8 km east of the Markt along the canal; the Oostpoort is signposted as a sight.
leads.verify_notes: Writing pass 2026-10-08: findable only by the species tell. The register pin falls between two crowns on the lawn (~6 m SW, ~10 m N) and no source says which is the ash or what the other tree is, so the recognition line leans on ash leaves and buds, which settles it only if the neighbour is not also an ash. Not made fully findable: needs a photograph of the trunk or a reader report naming which crown. Story asks the reader. Kept location_precision approximate with location_site as verified.
leads.story:
The gate is the famous one, but the ash on the lawn beside it is no medieval relic: the national register of monumental trees puts its planting between 1880 and 1890, centuries after the gate itself was built. That band makes the tree about 140 years old, give or take a decade, and it is the only date anybody has published for it.

It stands on a small municipal lawn by the canal at the Oostpoort quay, a plantsoen in the register's own word, listed as open to visit and visible from the path. The register records it as a single tree and says nothing about who planted it or why.

Surviving this long as an ash is its own small achievement. Ash dieback, a fungus that reached Europe in the 1990s, has been killing ashes across the continent, the Netherlands included. The most recent aerial photograph shows the crowns on this lawn still in leaf.

One honest caveat. The register's pin falls between two trees on the lawn, one a few metres south-west and one a little further north, and nobody has yet said which of them is the ash. If you stand there, the leaves settle it: an ash carries its leaflets in opposite pairs along a single stalk. Tell us which one it is, and send a photograph if you take one.
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, small leaflets in opposite pairs along one stalk, and black buds in winter. It stands on the small lawn by the canal at the Oostpoort, one of two trees the pin falls between.
